overview: The kingdom of Pamplona, later called Navarre, linked communities on both sides of the Pyrenees. Royal government, pilgrimage routes and towns left a rich written record. Its atlas interval 1000 to 1530 spans both independent monarchy and the conquest beginning in 1512; the single outline cannot represent every later division between Upper and Lower Navarre.

periods.title: The medieval kingdom
periods.summary: A kingdom with courts, towns, religious houses and routes across the Pyrenees developed its own legal institutions. Its origins precede the first atlas snapshot.

periods.title: Conquest and divided outcomes
periods.summary: Military campaigns began in 1512. Upper Navarre entered the Castilian crown in 1515 while the northern kingdom followed a different political path.

sections.title: A court with gardens and practical government

items.text: Charles III and Queen Eleanor transformed Olite’s palace during his 1387 to 1425 reign. Its irregular towers, rooms and gardens grew into a complex royal residence. This was exceptional courtly luxury, not a model of the typical Navarrese family home.

The municipality names Martín Périz of Estella as a master of masonry and Lope “el Barbicano,” a Muslim craftsman from Tudela, for carpentry. Named workers make the palace more than an anonymous royal achievement; different skills and communities helped create it.

Water from the Cidacos was raised with a bucket mechanism to the reservoir tower and distributed through lead pipes to gardens and fountains. The royal greenery depended on engineering and maintenance, not a naturally self-watering castle.

Olite’s court kept a menagerie including lions, a camel and an ostrich, as well as birds and hunting animals. These creatures advertised wealth and connections. Their presence does not tell us how comfortably the animals lived.

The Fuero General was compiled in the thirteenth century in Navarro-Aragonese. No author is securely identified, and it gained authority gradually through judicial use. A legal tradition could develop through repeated copying and practice rather than one dramatic founding decree.

Codex A1, a fourteenth-century copy of the Fuero, uses black and red ink and includes Philip III’s 1330 amendment. This particular book makes change visible: law was revised, not simply frozen forever in a medieval manuscript.

sections.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet

items.text: At Roncesvalles, the bishop of Pamplona organized a brotherhood of clergy and laypeople to care for pilgrims in 1127. The institution expanded during the 1130s. Hospitality at a mountain crossing meant dealing with travelers’ practical needs, not only maintaining a church.

Kings, nobles, bishops and grateful pilgrims gave the Roncesvalles institution land and income. Those endowments supported assistance. A hospital needed continuing resources; an impressive founding story alone could not feed the next group of tired travelers.

Surviving charters for Puente la Reina and Sangüesa from 1122, and San Saturnino in Pamplona from 1129, show how towns along the pilgrimage world were organized through written privileges. The archive also preserves an Irache charter concerning a pilgrims’ hospital.

Two officials, Martín de San Martín and Machín de Zalba, exchanged short letters on the same sheet, probably in 1416. The first asks about a tax reduction and then about dinner plans. Medieval office correspondence could switch from money to supper surprisingly quickly.

Zalba replied that he could not attend dinner because he had guests at home, then answered the tax question in Basque. The pair switched between Navarrese Romance and Basque. This proves these particular officials could use both, not that every inhabitant had the same language skills.

San Martín’s Basque farewell reads “jaunatiçula egun hon”: “May God give you a good day.” The spelling is preserved in the archive’s transcription of the probably 1416 letter. Basque was written here in Latin letters, within a document otherwise using Romance.

ending.text: Ferdinand’s invasion in 1512 began a prolonged conquest, not an instant disappearance of Navarre. Upper Navarre joined the Castilian crown in 1515 while retaining important institutions. Lower Navarre followed a separate path and was incorporated into the French monarchy in 1620. Communities and regional identities continued on both sides of the mountains.
